title: Vetala Story 9: The King and the Barber's Wife
summary: The Vetala said: 'O King! Listen to the tale of King Prasenajit and the Barber's Wife!'...
keywords: vetala story 9: the king and the barber's wife
full_text:
Recapturing the corpse from the branches, King Vikramaditya hoisted it onto his shoulders and marched through the cremation ground.

The Vetala said: 'O King! Listen to the tale of King Prasenajit and the Barber's Wife!'

In the city of Ayodhya lived an honest village barber named Sudharman and his devoted wife, Malati. Every morning, the barber shaved the king with extraordinary skill, gentle hands, and pleasant conversation, earning the monarch's warm favor.

The king's jealous chief minister, envious of the barber's intimacy with the sovereign, plotted his ruin. The minister whispered to the king: 'Sire, the barber boasts in the bazaar that his wife is more virtuous, pure, and dignified than the royal Queen herself!'

Offended by this reported insolence, the king summoned the barber's wife to the palace, intending to humiliate her before the court.

When Malati appeared before the throne, she was dressed in humble white cotton, devoid of jewels. Her eyes were downcast in modest reverence, and her countenance radiated such pure, unshakeable dignity and spiritual serenity that the entire court fell silent in awe.

The king attempted to provoke her with mocking questions: 'Woman! What ornament does an impoverished barber's wife possess that can compare to the diamonds of my Queen?'

Malati replied with gentle, fearless grace: 'Sire! The Queen possesses diamonds that were dug from the earth by slaves, bought with taxes, and can be stolen by thieves. My ornaments are three: truth in speech, contentment in poverty, and fidelity to my husband! Neither thieves can steal them, nor rust corrupt them, nor can the wrath of kings take them away!'

The king was humbled by her profound wisdom. He dismissed the jealous minister and showered the barber's household with fertile lands.

Here the Vetala asked: 'Tell me, King Vikramaditya: who was the truly noble figure in this contest—the king who repented, the minister who plotted, or the barber's wife who spoke truth? Answer, or your head will burst into fragments!'

Vikramaditya answered: 'The barber's wife was the true sovereign in that hall. True nobility belongs not to crowns and thrones, but to the unshakeable soul that speaks truth to power without fear, armed only with virtue and moral purity!'

'Rightly judged!' cried the Vetala, and flew back to his tree.
moral: A monarch who listens to flattering slanders against the humble stains the royal umbrella.
